content.heading: 7.2 Quadratic Forms
content.paragraph: Until now, our attention in this text has focused on linear equations, except for the sums of squares encountered in Chapter 6 when computing $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x}$. Such sums and more general expressions, called quadratic forms, occur frequently in applications of linear algebra to engineering (in design criteria and optimization) and signal processing (as output noise power). They also arise, for example, in physics (as potential and kinetic energy), differential geometry (as normal curvature of surfaces), economics (as utility functions), and statistics (in confidence ellipsoids). Some of the mathematical background for such applications flows easily from our work on symmetric matrices.

A quadratic form on ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is a function $Q$ defined on $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ whose value at a vector $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ can be computed by an expression of the form $Q\text{(}\textbf{x}\text{)} = \textbf{x}^{T}\mspace{-4mu} A\textbf{x}$, where $A$ is an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix. The matrix $A$ is called the matrix of the quadratic form.

The simplest example of a nonzero quadratic form is $Q\text{(}\textbf{x}\text{)} = \textbf{x}^{T}I\textbf{x} = \text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥}^{2}$. Examples 1 and 2 show the connection between any symmetric matrix $A$ and the quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}\mspace{-4mu} A\textbf{x}$.

content.paragraph: Example 4 illustrates the following theorem. The proof of the theorem was essentially given before Example 4.

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
The Principal Axes Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix. Then there is an orthogonal change of variable, $\textbf{x} = P\textbf{y}$, that transforms the quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ into a quadratic form $\textbf{y}^{T}D\textbf{y}$ with no cross-product term.

content.paragraph: The columns of $P$ in the theorem are called the principal axes of the quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$. The vector $\textbf{y}$ is the coordinate vector of $\textbf{x}$ relative to the orthonormal basis of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ given by these principal axes.

content.heading: Classifying Quadratic Forms
content.paragraph: When $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, the quadratic form $Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is a real-valued function with domain $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Figure 4 displays the graphs of four quadratic forms with domain $\text{ℝ}^{2}$. For each point $\textbf{x} = (x_{1},x_{2})$ in the domain of a quadratic form $Q$, the graph displays the point $(x_{1},x_{2},z)$ where $z = Q(\textbf{x})$. Notice that except at $\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$, the values of $Q(\textbf{x})$ are all positive in Figure 4(a) and all negative in Figure 4(d). The horizontal cross-sections of the graphs are ellipses in Figures 4(a) and 4(d) and hyperbolas in Figure 4(c).

content.paragraph: The simple $2 \times 2$ examples in Figure 4 illustrate the following definitions.

list.item: positive definite if Q(x)>0 for all x≠0,
negative definite if Q(x)<0 for all x≠0,
indefinite if Q(x) assumes both positive and negative values.

content.paragraph: Also, $Q$ is said to be positive semidefinite if $Q(\textbf{x}) \geq 0$ for all $\textbf{x}$, and to be negative semidefinite if $Q(\textbf{x}) \leq 0$ for all $\textbf{x}$. The quadratic forms in parts (a) and (b) of Figure 4 are both positive semidefinite, but the form in (a) is better described as positive definite.
Theorem5 characterizes some quadratic forms in terms of eigenvalues.

note.title: Theorem 5
note.heading: Theorem 5
Quadratic Forms and Eigenvalues
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix. Then a quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is

list.item: positive definite if and only if the eigenvalues of A are all positive,
negative definite if and only if the eigenvalues of A are all negative, or
indefinite if and only if A has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

content.paragraph: The classification of a quadratic form is often carried over to the matrix of the form. Thus a positive definite matrix ﻿$A$ is a symmetric matrix for which the quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is positive definite. Other terms, such as positive semidefinite matrix, are defined analogously.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: A fast way to determine whether a symmetric matrix $A$ is positive definite is to attempt to factor $A$ in the form $A = R^{T}R$, where $R$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal entries. (A slightly modified algorithm for an LU factorization is one approach.) Such a Cholesky factorization is possible if and only if $A$ is positive definite. See Supplementary Exercise 23 at the end of Chapter 7.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) The matrix of a quadratic form is a symmetric matrix.
(T/F) The expression $\text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥}^{2}$ is not a quadratic form.
(T/F) A quadratic form has no cross-product terms if and only if the matrix of the quadratic form is a diagonal matrix.
